slides.title: Part 1 — The one idea the whole field is built on
slides.body: Attention is the mechanism that replaced recurrence and convolution. Once you can read an attention heatmap and write the formula from memory, the rest of the transformer is bookkeeping. Spend real time here.

slides.title: What attention computes
slides.body:
Look at the heatmap. Each **row is a query** (a token asking a question), each **column is a key** (a token advertising itself). Brighter = stronger attention.

Notice the row for **`are`** — almost all its weight sits on **`cats`**. The verb has learned it must agree with its subject several tokens back. Nobody coded that rule; it emerged from training on grammatical text.

The whole point: every token gets to **look at every other token**, weighted by relevance, and blend their information in a *single* parallel operation. RNNs passed information one step at a time; attention has full reach at once.

slides.title: Three vectors per token: Q, K, V
slides.body:
Each token is projected three ways:

- **Query (Q):** "What am I looking for?"
- **Key (K):** "What do I offer?"
- **Value (V):** "What information do I carry?"

The score from token $i$ to token $j$ is the dot product $Q_i\cdot K_j$ — large when query and key align. Softmax turns scores into weights; the output is the weighted sum of values:

$$\text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$

Three matmuls and a softmax. That's the entire mechanism.

slides.title: Why divide by √d_k
slides.body:
If $Q$ and $K$ have dimension $d_k$ with unit-variance entries, the dot product $Q_i\cdot K_j$ has variance $\approx d_k$. For $d_k=64$ that's a standard deviation of 8 — large scores push softmax into a near one-hot regime where gradients vanish.

Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ rescales the scores back to unit variance, keeping softmax in its responsive range. It is a tiny constant with an outsized effect on whether the model trains at all — a recurring theme: numerical scaling is not a detail.

slides.title: A locality head
slides.body:
Different heads learn different patterns. This one shows a **locality bias** — each token attends mostly to its neighbors. Useful where nearby context dominates (syntax). Any trained transformer grows some heads like this.

Other heads learn long-range dependencies; many learn structures we still don't fully understand. Reverse-engineering them is the field of *mechanistic interpretability* — built entirely on the fact that these patterns are real and reproducible.

slides.title: A coreference pattern
slides.body:
Here the pronoun **`she`** attends back to its antecedent **`Maria`**. The model learned that pronouns need to know what they refer to, and attention is the mechanism that lets it look back.

In a real model this is a *circuit* spanning multiple heads and layers (Olsson et al., 2022, traced an analogous induction mechanism), but the takeaway stands: trained attention discovers linguistic structure on its own.

question.question: What does the matrix product Q · Kᵀ produce?
options: An n×n matrix where entry (i, j) is the similarity score between query i and key j
A scalar — the total attention magnitude
An n-dimensional probability vector over keys
A new embedding for each token in a different space
question.explanation: Q is [n, d_k] and K is [n, d_k], so Q · Kᵀ is [n, n]. Entry (i, j) is the dot product of query i with key j — a raw similarity. After ÷√d_k and softmax (row-wise) it becomes the attention-weight matrix.

question.question: Remove the 1/√d_k scaling for large d_k. What is the most likely failure?
options: Dot products grow large, softmax saturates toward one-hot, gradients vanish, training stalls
The output is no longer a weighted average
Nothing — the scaling is purely cosmetic
question.explanation: Unscaled scores have variance ≈ d_k. Big logits make softmax extremely peaked; its gradient is near zero almost everywhere, so the attention layer stops learning. The √d_k divisor keeps scores at unit variance and softmax responsive.

question.question: Write the scaled dot-product attention formula (use softmax, Q, K, V, d_k).
question.hint: Scores = QKᵀ, scaled by 1/√d_k, softmaxed, then applied to V.
question.explanation: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵀ / √d_k) · V. Scores from Q·Kᵀ, scaled for numerical stability, normalized by softmax into weights, then used to take a weighted sum of the value vectors.

slides.title: What's next
slides.body:
You can now read an attention map and write the formula. The follow-ups make it practical:

- **[Self-attention](/wiki/self-attention)** — Q, K, V from the *same* sequence; every token attends to every other.
- **[Multi-head attention](/wiki/multi-head-attention)** — many attention computations in parallel, each a different subspace, so one layer learns many patterns.
- **[Causal masking](/wiki/masked-self-attention)** — mask the future so autoregressive generation can't cheat.

Everything important in a transformer happens in attention; the rest is plumbing around it.
